title: Mayonnaise
subtitle: smooth, glossy home-made mayonnaise
excerpt: Home-made mayonnaise takes about 5 minutes and tastes far better than shop-bought. The method is the same as hollandaise but cold: egg yolk, mustard, and acid form a base, then oil is whisked in slowly until you have a thick, creamy emulsion.
sourceNotes: Mayonnaise is believed to have originated in Mahon, Minorca, in the 18th century, though the French claim its invention too. It became one of the most widely used condiments in Europe and North America by the 20th century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days.

content.text: The key is patience at the start. The first tablespoon of oil must be added drop by drop while whisking. Once the emulsion is established, you can add the oil in a thin stream. Going too fast at the beginning is what causes the sauce to split.

items.prepNote: or use a neutral oil for a milder flavour

content.text: Put the egg yolks, mustard, and a pinch of salt in a bowl. Whisk together for 30 seconds.
Start adding the oil one drop at a time, whisking constantly. After about 2 tablespoons, the mixture should look thick and glossy.
Now you can add the oil in a very thin, slow stream, whisking all the time.
Once all the oil is incorporated, whisk in the lemon juice and vinegar. Taste and season.
Transfer to a jar and refrigerate. Use within 5 days.

items.symptom: Mayonnaise has split and looks oily
items.cause: Oil added too fast at the start
items.fix: Put a fresh egg yolk in a clean bowl and slowly whisk the split mayo into it, drop by drop.
Whisk in a teaspoon of cold water or lemon juice to loosen.

content.text: Mayonnaise is thought to have originated on the Spanish island of Minorca in the 18th century, possibly following the French capture of Mahon in 1756. Whether French or Spanish in origin, it became one of the defining sauces of European cooking. It is now one of the most consumed condiments in the world. Home-made is worth the small extra effort.
